❯ Without using any tools, write a detailed 800-word essay on the history of terminal multiplexers, covering screen, tmux and zellij. Take your time and think it through first.

● From Detachable Sessions to Tiled Workspaces: A Short History of Terminal Multiplexers

  Every terminal multiplexer exists to solve one stubborn problem: the Unix pseudoterminal is bound to whoever opened it. Run a long compile over a dial-up line or a flaky SSH tunnel, lose the link, and SIGHUP takes the work with it. In
  the 1980s, when a user typically had one physical terminal on a serial line into a shared machine, this was doubly painful — one screen, one shell, one connection, no recovery. The multiplexer's insight was to insert a persistent process
  between the terminal and the programs running in it. The program talks to a pty owned by a long-lived daemon; the human attaches and detaches at will. Everything since has been refinement of that idea.

  The first widely used implementation was screen, written by Oliver Laumann and Carsten Bormann at the Technical University of Berlin and posted to comp.sources.unix in 1987. It offered the full pattern immediately: multiple windows on
  one physical terminal, a copy/scrollback buffer, and — the killer feature — detach and reattach, letting a session survive logout and be picked up later from a different terminal entirely. It handled serial ports and hardware terminal
  quirks, and supported multiuser attachment, making it a natural tool for remote assistance and teaching. Screen became GNU software and was adopted almost universally; for two decades, "leave it running in screen" was standard sysadmin
  advice. Its Ctrl-A prefix key entered muscle memory so deeply that later tools still ship compatibility bindings for it.

  Screen also became a case study in software aging. The codebase carried an enormous amount of terminal-compatibility history, configuration lived in an idiosyncratic .screenrc language, and development slowed dramatically: version 4.0.3
  landed in 2006 and the next substantive release did not arrive until 2014, which finally shipped proper split panes — by then a feature people had been getting elsewhere for years. Splits were not persisted across detach, scripting was
  awkward, and the internal architecture made new features expensive to add.

  tmux, started by Nicholas Marriott and first released in late 2007, was a deliberate rewrite of the concept rather than an incremental improvement. Licensed under the permissive ISC license — which mattered to the BSD world, where
  screen's GPL was unwelcome in the base system — it was imported into OpenBSD in 2009 and has shipped there ever since. Architecturally, tmux is explicit about the client-server split that screen implied: a single server process owns the
  sessions and the ptys, and clients connect over a Unix domain socket. The decisive design choice was making everything a command. Key bindings, configuration lines, and the tmux binary itself all funnel into one command language, so tmux
  new-window -n build, tmux split-window -h, and tmux send-keys work identically from a keybinding, a config file, or a shell script. Panes were first-class from early on, layouts were persistent, and a later "control mode" let terminal
  emulators such as iTerm2 render tmux sessions as native tabs.

  That scriptability produced an ecosystem screen never had. Session managers like tmuxinator and tmuxp declare whole project workspaces in YAML; the tmux plugin manager (tpm) distributes plugins such as tmux-resurrect, which restores
  sessions across reboots; tmate forked tmux into an instant pair-programming service; vim-tmux-navigator unified pane and split movement. Paired with mosh for roaming connections, tmux became the default remote-development substrate for a
  generation of developers, and its Ctrl-B prefix — widely rebound to Ctrl-A or Ctrl-Space — a fixture of shared dotfiles.

  The cost of that power was discoverability. tmux is effectively modal and undocumented at the point of use: nothing on screen tells you what the prefix key does, and productive use begins with copying someone else's config. Zellij, begun
  around 2020 by Aram Drevekenin under the name Mosaic and renamed for Moroccan mosaic tilework, targets exactly that gap. Written in Rust, it ships with a visible status bar that advertises its modes and keybindings, sensible defaults
  intended to be usable before configuration, floating and stacked panes, and layouts declared in KDL (after an early YAML iteration). Its most distinctive bet is a plugin system built on WebAssembly and WASI: plugins are sandboxed wasm
  modules that can be written in any language targeting that runtime, and much of Zellij's own UI — the status bar, the session manager, the tab bar — is implemented as plugins on the same interface. It has spent years in the 0.x series,
  iterating fast rather than freezing an API.

  Meanwhile the ground has shifted underneath all three. Terminal emulators like WezTerm and kitty now provide their own tabs, splits, and even remote session persistence; containers, editors with integrated terminals, and cloud dev
  environments absorb some of the same needs; minimal tools like dtach and abduco strip the idea back to bare detachment. Yet the multiplexer endures, because the pty and the fragile connection endure. Nearly forty years after screen, the
  abstraction it introduced — a session that outlives the terminal watching it — remains one of Unix's most quietly durable ideas.
